uncited: Traversal Acceleration refers to a family of techniques that utilize hierarchical data structures, primarily octrees, to optimize the access patterns and computational cost of volume rendering and geometric queries.
It solves the problem of excessive processing time caused by traversing large, sparse, or complex volumetric datasets by enabling the skipping of empty or irrelevant regions.

What sets this family apart from its siblings is the specific application of acceleration structures (such as min-max octrees, summed area tables, or shadow grids) to bypass expensive per-voxel computations during rendering or intersection tests, rather than just storing the data itself.
The parent article [Octree-based structures](2792-octree-based-structures.md) defines the shared mechanism for all structures in this family.

Traversal Acceleration builds on [Octree-based structures](2792-octree-based-structures.md) by adding specific metadata or auxiliary structures to the octree nodes to facilitate faster culling or aggregation during the traversal phase.
Octree structure: Root node contains entire volume; has eight child nodes, each representing 1/8 of the volume.
Storage cost: two bits per light source per voxel.
